title: Alias-aware temporal pinning with performance-profile constraints for model selection
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Customers need deterministic and auditable model selection semantics when they pin models using different identifier forms (alias/tag, semver ranges, commit hashes). Current SDK contracts allow pins by raw identifier but do not consider alias lifecycle (alias reassignment), temporal stability windows, or whether the selected model meets published performance profile constraints (e.g., 95th-percentile latency under threshold). This leads to live-site surprises during rollouts and makes it hard to guarantee SLOs for different customer tiers.

Goal: Define and implement an SDK/API model-resolution algorithm that is alias-aware (resolves aliases to a concrete release by considering alias history and optional time windows), supports pin-by-tag/semver/hash, enforces performance-profile constraints at selection time (optionally), and emits rich audit metadata for downstream observability and debugging. Ensure a backward-compatible migration path for existing pin semantics and small SDK changes for client apps to opt into stricter semantics.

Scope: API + SDK client-side resolver, runtime acceptance checks, audit log fields, docs and migration guide. This ticket focuses on the semantics and SDK changes; runtime enforcement will be a follow-up runtime ticket (see dependencies).
proposal:
High-level approach broken into parts: 
1) Alias-aware resolution: When a client pins to an alias (e.g., 'stable', 'nightly', 'redwood:v2-latest'), the SDK resolver will resolve to the concrete model ref using a deterministic precedence that can be time-windowed. If the client supplies a 'stability_window' (ISO date range) the resolver will select the most recent concrete release whose alias assignment overlapped that window. This prevents alias-flapping surprises when aliases are reattached.

2) Identifier forms: Support three canonical input types: 'alias' (string label), 'semver' (exact or range expresion like ^1.2.0), and 'commit' (full or short hash). Semver range resolution will use release metadata (published semver) and prefer releases marked 'serving-ready'.

3) Performance-profile filtering: Clients may pass an optional 'profile_requirements' object (SDK level) naming constraints like max_p95_latency_ms, max_cost_per_1k_tokens_usd, or min_throughput_rps. The resolver will consult the model catalog's published performance profiles (cached locally and refreshed) and only consider concrete releases that satisfy all constraints. If none match, resolution fails fast with structured error and suggested fallbacks.

4) Fallback semantics: Resolution inputs can include an ordered 'fallbacks' list. When primary resolution fails (alias not resolvable to eligible release, or profile mismatch), the resolver tries fallback selectors in order. The SDK will also expose a 'dry_run' mode that returns the resolution decision without issuing traffic.

5) Audit metadata and observability: Every resolution must return a small audit tuple: resolved_ref, resolution_path (list of candidate refs tried, as strings), reason (e.g., 'alias->release', 'semver-match', 'commit-exact'), profile_check: pass|fail and matched_profile_id, timestamp, and a stable resolution_hash for caching and telemetry. The runtime will log the tuple (follow-up task).

6) Backwards compatibility: Default behavior when the client uses existing simple 'model' string remains unchanged (legacy resolver). New optional fields are additive on the SDK call signature (see API surface).
api_surface:
Proposed SDK signature (pseudocode): 

resolveModel({
  model_selector: string, // alias | semver | commit (same field as today)
  selector_type?: 'alias' | 'semver' | 'commit', // optional disambiguator
  stability_window?: string, // e.g. '2025-01-01/2025-01-31' ISO range
  profile_requirements?: [ 'max_p95_latency_ms:400', 'max_cost_per_1k_tokens_usd:0.02' ],
  fallbacks?: [ {model_selector, selector_type} ],
  dry_run?: boolean
}) -> {
  resolved_ref: string,
  resolution_path: [string],
  profile_check: 'pass'|'fail',
  matched_profile: string,
  resolution_hash: string
}

Errors: 
- RESOLUTION_NO_MATCH (404-like) with details about candidates tried and why they failed.
- PROFILE_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION (422) listing violated constraints and suggested alternative selectors.

Implementation notes: the SDK will maintain a cache of model-catalog entries and performance profiles; TTL and invalidation guided by server ETags. When strict profile enforcement is used, the client may optionally request an immediate runtime probe (server-side quick-check) — this expands to the runtime acceptance ticket.

Example usage: 
- Pin by alias with window: resolveModel({ model_selector: 'stable', selector_type: 'alias', stability_window: '2025-01-01/2025-01-31', profile_requirements: ['max_p95_latency_ms:200'] })
- Pin by semver range: resolveModel({ model_selector: '^2.3.0', selector_type: 'semver' })
acceptance_criteria:
1) SDK exposes resolveModel API with optional stability_window, profile_requirements, fallbacks, and dry_run flags.
2) Alias resolution honors stability_window and returns the concrete model ref plus resolution_path and resolution_hash.
3) Profile constraints are evaluated against cached performance profiles; when constraints are unmet an explicit PROFILE_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION error is returned (with candidates list).
4) Fallback chain is exercised in order and resolution returns first eligible candidate.
5) Default legacy behavior (single model string without extras) is unchanged.
6) Unit tests for semver-range resolution, alias-window selection, profile filtering, and fallback order.
7) Integration test (SDK + mock catalog) demonstrating dry_run returns same decision as full resolution without side effects.

Manual review: API docs, migration guide, and a short RFC entry in Confluence.
implementation_notes:
Work will be split between: 
- SDK resolver (primary) — implement deterministic algorithm, cache layer, and errors.
- SDK docs + migration guide — examples and recommended patterns.
- Runtime integration (follow-up) — acceptance probes, server-side profile checks, and audit logging.

Performance considerations: profile checks must be fast — prefer evaluating against cached numeric metrics. Large semver catalogs require efficient candidate filtering (pre-index by semver major/minor). Cache TTL defaults: 5 minutes for catalog, 1 minute for profiles for hosted tier; dedicated/private deployments can configure TTLs.

Edge cases & trade-offs: 
- Alias reassignment windows: using a stability_window avoids surprising rebinds but increases complexity for users specifying windows; recommend providing sensible defaults (e.g., resolve to earliest serving-ready release within last 72 hours).
- Strong profile enforcement can increase failure surface for clients that rely on best-effort pins; keep enforcement opt-in.
- Semver range semantics: follow npm-style precedence but only consider releases labeled 'serving-ready' to avoid selecting untested builds.

Security/Compliance: resolution audit tuples must be logged with customer context only when permitted (obey data residency and PII rules). This is why security_review_required is true.
